SystemSketch · golden 10 · implementation

The Loop region, with the item on an ordinary solid cable

Golden 10's grammar was settled across two days of babble. This is the vertical slice of it: a for becomes a frame-like region whose header is an operator, and the element it emits travels on a plain solid cable — because dotted already means one turn late.

tldraw 5.3.2 · stock 928 lines in src/loop 12/12 real-browser checks branch track/loop-region from 1e03d24

What "B solid drop" actually required

B is a claim about one cable, but the cable had nothing to hang off: there was no Loop region. So the slice is the region, and B falls out of one decision inside it.

The grammar saidWhat the code does
The header is an operator The collection lands ON the header through a real Iterable inlet — the same move a Branch makes with its controlling value — and the header emits the element from a real outlet directly beneath it. Nothing passes through the region on its way to a Block.
A real port, not a derived one Both are ordinary entries in the connection layer's port table, welded by the same binding, the same rules and the same paint as a Block's. The drawing stays wirable.
The item cable is solid This is the whole of B, and it cost nothing. The item outlet is an output port, and an output welds an ordinary temporal: data connection, which paints solid. Dotted is temporal: delayed — one turn late — and the loop's back cable uses it. The element is this turn's value, so it must not share that line. No new cable kind was needed to say so.
Centred title An operator's name belongs over the middle of it. The layout keeps it clear of the iterable label on the left and the turn chip on the right.

The one seam that had drifted

Adding a third port host produced a cable tldraw silently refused to bind. The drag died with no error, no console entry and no failed assertion — the state machine simply fell back to idle.

// ConnectionShapeUtil.canBind, before
return bindingType === 'connection'
    && fromShapeType === CONNECTION_SHAPE_TYPE
    && (toShapeType === 'block' || toShapeType === 'branch')

isPortHostShape kept one list of hosts and canBind spelled out another by hand. They agreed for two hosts and disagreed for three. Both now read one exported PORT_HOST_SHAPE_TYPES, so a fourth host can only be forgotten in one place.

Two things the first screenshot decided

Neither was visible in a unit test, and both were obvious the moment the acceptance journey painted a real board.

  • The item label moved below its dot. It sat beside the dot, on exactly the row a cable leaves along — so the first cable drawn from that port struck the word through.
  • The item port moved onto the wall. It was inset on the header's top edge; it now sits at the header's bottom corner directly under Iterable, which is where Zach drew it.

Proof

npm run check is green — tsc, 792 vitest and 74 Python tests, including nine new unit tests over the layout and the port projection. That is necessary and not sufficient; the claim is about a real board.

The visual QA sweep, and what it found

npm run test:loop-qa is a capture rig rather than a pass/fail journey. It drives the region through the cases that actually break a canvas UI and writes one frame and one machine-readable observation each, so every frame can be looked at rather than trusted. Three real defects came out of looking.

DefectWhat it was, and what fixed it
The header had three tenants and no allocation The type labels, the centred title and the turn chip all wanted the same pixels. At 300px the title ran straight through the chip; a long turn string crowded the region's edge and nothing truncated. The row is now allocated — labels get a bounded budget, the title centres in the band that survives, and the chip yields first because it reports a live state while the title identifies the region. All three truncate with an ellipsis and keep the full string as a tooltip. The old assertion on the title's exact x is replaced by a property over six widths × three turn strings × two type lengths.
A tap on a Loop port did nothing …while a drag from the same dot worked. anchorFaceForScope spelled its hosts out by hand — isBlockShape || isBranchShape — exactly as canBind had, so the picker asked for a face, got null, and bailed with no error. Second instance of one bug: a hand-written host list. The rig only caught it because it ran the same tap on a Block port as a control.
The picker opened the wrong way Off to the right, on top of the header the cable had just left. The offered Block now goes where the cable points, which for a header port is down — the same elbowSide the router reads.

One flaw was in the rig, not the product. The tap-port case left a picker open, and the export case that followed reported the region's chrome missing from the SVG — a defect that vanished when the case ran alone. Each case now cancels and resets first. A rig that lies about a real feature is worse than no rig.

Left as a design question, not a bug. The fan-out frame shows one element feeding three Blocks as three parallel horizontal runs — the bundle of parallel arrows this whole thread started by rejecting. It is correct and it is ugly, and it wants a decision before anyone draws it for real.

The types are authorable now

You said a header port carries a type you can define. It did not: the two types were baked into the shape's defaults and reachable only from code. There is now a Loop inspector in the same idiom as the Block's and the Branch's — Loop (title), Header ports (the two types, each with its colour chip), and Turn (what the chip reads, empty to hide it). No name field appears anywhere, because a header port has no name.

The panel existed but nothing could reach it. The inspector dock auto-opens when its subject key changes, and that key knew about Blocks, Branches and cables — not regions. So a selected Loop opened nothing, and the generic selection pill's Inspect button was not rendering either. Selecting a Loop now opens its panel exactly as selecting a Block does. This is the third time in this track that a hand-maintained list of subjects left the Loop out — after canBind and anchorFaceForScope. Worth watching for a fourth.

The load-bearing test. A cable is welded to a port by ID, so retyping a port must not disturb the ID. The journey retypes both header ports through the inspector with real clicks and keystrokes and then asserts the painted labels changed, both cables are still attached, and there are zero orphaned bindings. That is check L10, and it is why setLoopPortType writes the type and nothing else.

Known, and deliberately left

The item cable's elbow route laps the region. The binding is right and the line style is right; only the path is ugly. The live paint asks every port to leave rightward and escape its shape's box, and a region's box is the whole region. Fixing it means changing box construction shared with every Block cable, which belongs in its own slice behind the routing corpus rather than bolted onto this one. A card on the review board says so.

Not built, and not pretended: the faded zero-iterations arm — you called for it and it is right, but the fade has to be authored state on the region rather than something the canvas derives, and choosing that state is a design decision I will not invent; a live iteration counter (turn is a plain string prop, so the chip renders whatever it is given); break, else, and nested loops.

A UX question the QA sweep raised. A selected Loop takes the chrome's generic selection pill — appearance controls it has no styles for, plus Tidy/Organize, plus Inspect — while a Branch gets a mini-menu of its own. What belongs on a Loop's pill is a decision, not a defect, so it is unchanged.
